UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.​ ​             ​       )​       ​       Docket No. ER26-1479-000
​     ​      ​       ​       ​             ​       )​


                       COMMENTS OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

           Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)1, the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”), respectfully

submits these formal comments in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) February

23, 2026 tariff filing in compliance (“PJM’s Compliance Filings”) to the Commission's

December 18, 2025 order.2


     I.​   Introduction

           DCC respectfully submits these comments on PJM’s proposed revisions to the PJM Open

Access Transmission Tariff to comply with the Commission’s directives in its Order to Show

Cause to (1) revise its behind-the-meter generation Tariff provisions, (2) establish three new

transmission services for Eligible Customers seeking to take service on behalf of Co- Located

Load, and (3) revise its necessary studies processes, among other changes. This proceeding arises

at a pivotal moment for the nation’s energy grid and digital infrastructure, as regional grid

operators face rising demand, constrained transmission capacity, increased local opposition to

infrastructure development, and growing uncertainty around supply adequacy.




1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC 61,217, (2025) (Order to Show Cause).

                                                        1
         DCC is the membership organization for the U.S. data center industry, representing

leading data center owners and operators with infrastructure and employees across the country.3

DCC member companies are making significant, multi-billion dollar investments in America’s

infrastructure. These investments support hundreds of thousands of quality jobs across the nation

and contribute billions of dollars in local, state, and federal tax revenue, providing consistent

funding for important community priorities like public safety, education, and transportation.

        Between 2017 and 2023, the data center industry’s total contribution to U.S. GDP was

$3.5 trillion. In 2023, the U.S. data center industry directly employed more than 600,000 workers

and supported 4.7 million jobs in total. The sector generated $404 billion in total labor income

and contributed $162.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2023.4

        Data centers are foundational to the modern economy and the digital services on which it

depends. They support essential services across nearly every sector, including finance,

healthcare, education, communications, manufacturing, defense, and government. As the

backbone of the nation’s digital infrastructure, data centers host the computing platforms that

power artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads, cybersecurity systems that protect

critical institutions, and data processing capabilities relied upon by federal agencies and national

security entities. These facilities support real-time digital operations that are now inseparable

from the functioning of core public and private systems.

        In recent years, energy demand has accelerated—driven by Artificial Intelligence (“AI”)

development, cloud computing, electrification of buildings, industry and transportation,

hydrogen fuel production, and the reshoring of U.S. advanced manufacturing. This has created a

                                                       2
 step change in electricity needs, particularly in regions like PJM, where demand is outpacing

outdated planning frameworks. Data center operators are responding with urgency—but face

growing constraints from generator interconnection delays, opaque infrastructure planning, and

limited transparency into available capacity.

        In this context, co-location of load with generation—whether front-of-the-meter or

behind-the-meter—is a pragmatic, common, and commercially legitimate strategy to secure

timely access to power as markets grapple with years-long interconnection queue backlogs.

These arrangements provide critical flexibility and efficiency, enabling data center developers to

meet emerging needs on faster timelines and without undue reliance on already-congested grid

infrastructure should they pursue this option.

        The Commission has the opportunity in this proceeding to ensure PJM is complying with

its Order to Show Cause and ensure co-location arrangements are a viable pathway in the future

for large load customers. To assist in that effort, these comments: (1) provide an overview of

PJM’s Compliance Filing; and (2) point to the unworkable nature of PJM’s compliance filing and

recommend solutions.


 II.​   PJM’s Compliance Filing

        In response to the Order to Show Cause, PJM filed revisions to its Tariff addressing

Retail Behind-the-Meter Generation (BTMG) and transmission service for large loads. The

proposal establishes a 50 MW materiality threshold for Retail BTMG, under which facilities with

a cumulative nameplate rating of 50 MW or less may qualify for retail netting treatment. PJM

indicated this threshold aligns with its definition of large load additions and reflects stakeholder

feedback. The filing also includes an emergency generation exemption, which excludes on-site

backup generators from the BTMG calculation so that facilities such as data centers can maintain


                                                  3
 diesel or natural gas backup generation for reliability purposes, provided those units are not used

for routine retail netting.

        PJM also proposes grandfathering provisions intended to protect existing arrangements.

Facilities with BTMG capacity exceeding 50 MW may be permanently grandfathered if they

operate under a contractual arrangement that was in effect before December 18, 2025. In

addition, the proposal exempts certain Qualifying Facilities that achieved operational status

before that date under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978. PJM stated these

provisions are designed to avoid disrupting existing investments while establishing clearer limits

for future projects.

        Finally, PJM proposed three new transmission service options for Eligible Customers.

Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service would allow customers to receive service up to a

defined maximum megawatt level. Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service would

allow co-located loads to withdraw power from the grid on an as-needed and as-available basis.

PJM also proposed Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (“Interim NITS”), which

would allow customers that have requested full Network Integration Transmission Service

(“NITS”) to begin operations on a non-firm, interruptible basis while transmission upgrades

necessary for long-term firm service are constructed. These proposed service options form the

basis of DCC’s concerns discussed below.


III.​   DCC Comments

        Co-location is a commercial arrangement that enables load and generation to be sited

together in ways that facilitate timely power delivery, reduce dependence on constrained

transmission systems, and enhance investment certainty. These arrangements involve

sophisticated engineering, contractual, and regulatory compliance components. When properly


                                                 4
 structured, they can preserve and improve overall grid reliability while expanding the set of

viable options available to new large loads.

           DCC has previously urged the Commission to direct PJM to develop clear, enforceable

tariff language that affirms the permissibility of multiple co-location configurations, including

those where load is served directly from a generation resource located on or near the same site.

The Commission did just that with its Order to Show Cause. Tariff clarity is essential to reduce

unnecessary disputes, avoid case-by-case confusion, and enable transmission providers to

process interconnection and load addition requests efficiently and predictably. The Commission

provided clear guidance to PJM on how PJM should implement the Commission’s co-location

order and facilitate the interconnection of new large loads such as data centers.

           In its filing, PJM states it “understands the importance of, and remains committed to,

advancing our nation’s leadership in connecting large loads, including supporting the

development of Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) infrastructure. PJM continues to work with its

members to support efforts to accelerate the speed and increase the scale with which the United

States can build the next generation of AI infrastructure, especially the necessary capacity to

support this load while also ensuring reliability and fair treatment for all users of the grid.” 5

           However, PJM’s proposal falls short of the Commission’s clear directive and the goals

PJM itself identifies. As a result, the data center industry is left without viable pathways to bring

solutions that accelerate the interconnection of critical load and generation and address the

ongoing capacity shortfalls in PJM. FERC’s direction to provide a materiality threshold, which

PJM set at 50 MW for BTMG, was to coincide with a suite of changes that also included a viable

and efficient co-location path that is not BTMG. But PJM’s compliance filing leaves several core

operational questions unanswered. For example, PJM’s proposed Interim NITS will be difficult
5
    PJM’s Compliance Filing at 2.

                                                    5
 for customers to rely upon unless several key issues are resolved. As proposed, the framework

leaves significant uncertainty regarding how the service would operate in practice, including the

interaction between Interim NITS and co-located generation arrangements. This uncertainty

creates substantial risk for customers considering major infrastructure investments and may

render the service largely unusable in its current form.


             a.​ Interim NITS Is Not Workable If Customers Cannot Use Co-Located
                 Generation During Curtailment

        The proposal leaves unresolved a critical question regarding whether customers receiving

Interim NITS may take energy from a co-located generator when their network service is

curtailed. Interim NITS is intended to provide an incentive for load to bring generation behind

the meter in exchange for getting energized more quickly while awaiting for transmission

upgrades. However, PJM has proposed to prohibit customers from relying on co-located

generation during curtailment events. In its January 23, 2026 Preliminary Proposal, PJM outlined

its curtailment procedures for Interim NITS. As part of those procedures, PJM stated “[i]f

curtailed, EC cannot take energy from co-located generator.”6 This is unworkable because

curtailment should limit use of the grid, not prevent the customer from using the co-located

resource it supplied, which supports Interim NITS in the first place. If the customer cannot use

that generation during curtailment, Interim NITS provides no practical value.

        Maintaining such a limitation would significantly undermine the operational value of

co-located generation arrangements. If co-located customers are expected to bring new resources

to market, they should have access to those resources in time of curtailment.

        Further, PJM must define the trigger, scope, and sequence of Interim NITS curtailment

with respect to the operational limitations identified in the study and should not be able to curtail

 load for unrelated broader resource adequacy concerns, particularly where the colocated load has

brought sufficient new supply to meet its demand. Curtailment direction unrelated to the result of

the NITS studies should be outside the scope of this proceeding.


           b.​ PJM Must Establish a Defined Process and Timeline for Necessary Studies
               and CIR Review

        In its filing PJM also provides guidance on interconnection rules for existing generators.

PJM proposes any existing power plant seeking to serve co-located load must now go through a

formal Necessary Studies process, reduce its Capacity Interconnection Rights (CIRs)

accordingly, and execute a new Generation Interconnection Agreement before a single megawatt

of co-located load can be served. However, clearer interconnection rules for existing generators

also require more concrete timelines to review and approve these Necessary Studies and CIR

revisions. PJM also needs to account for CIRs going to the specific co-located customer in a

manner that doesn't force a generator to reduce more CIRs than necessary, which may happen

when this is done on a 3-year look ahead. Clarity on the timeline for these reviews is needed so

large load customers can plan their investment accordingly.


           c.​ PJM’s Effective Date Should Be Earlier

        PJM has proposed an effective date of June 1, 2029 for these new transmission services.

Given the immediate need to connect new generation and load in PJM, this presumably means

that PJM cannot start studying these innovative solutions for over three years. PJM should work

with stakeholders to implement workable solutions in a timely manner that ensures these services

can meet the immediate need within the PJM region. As discussed, PJM still has much work

to-do to refine these services, but the goal should be to implement needed reforms earlier than

2029.


                                                 7
            d.​ PJM Should Provide Greater Transparency Regarding how Customers Will
               Transition from Interim NITS to NITS

       While Interim NITS is intended to function as a temporary solution, the proposal does not

provide clear timelines to co-location customers to expect to be transitioned to NITS or how long

customers may be required to rely on the interim framework. Without clear timelines, Interim

NITS could persist indefinitely, creating regulatory and operational uncertainty for customers

making long-term investments in load and generation resources.


IV.​   Conclusion

       DCC appreciates FERC’s leadership and innovation in pushing forward new transmission

services in PJM. At this pivotal moment in the global AI race and America’s economic growth,

FERC has a critical role to play in ensuring these services are not simply theoretical, but can

actually be implemented in practice in a timely manner. In light of the significant policy and

operational questions, several issues require further clarification and development. Accordingly,

the Commission should require PJM to further clarify and revise its proposal to: (1) confirm that

an Interim NITS customer may continue to use co-located generation when network service is

curtailed; (2) establish a defined process and timeline for Necessary Studies and associated CIR

revisions, and to ensure that any CIR reductions are tailored to the co-located service actually

being provided; (4) PJM should endeavor to implement needed reforms in a timely manner; and

(5) provide greater transparency regarding how customers will transition from Interim NITS to

full NITS. These matters, as well as additional concerns that may arise through stakeholder

engagement, should be more fully addressed by PJM to ensure that the resulting framework is

workable and provides sufficient certainty for customers considering major infrastructure

investments.



                                                 8
        DCC looks forward to actively participating in the paper hearing proceeding and

contributing to the development of a comprehensive record on these issues. Given the

consequential nature of these issues and the scale of investments that will be affected, the

Commission should take the time to get the framework right. A thoughtful and well-developed

record will help ensure that any resulting policies provide regulatory certainty while maintaining

the reliability and integrity of the regional transmission system.


Respectfully submitted,
